questions.q: Why does a production model with no recoverable lineage become a bigger problem than it would be for a research run?
options: It doesn't -- lineage only matters during research, not after deployment
A production incident months later is a much higher-stakes version of 'what produced this number,' turning every follow-up question into an investigation instead of a lookup
Production models cannot be retrained regardless of lineage
Lineage information is automatically embedded in model weights
questions.explain: Lesson 16's rule -- recover the exact code behind a result -- matters even more in production, where a regression or retraining question months later has no one around to just ask.

questions.q: Why should the eval harness be wired into CI as a regression test rather than left behind in the research repo?
options: CI pipelines run faster than research clusters
Without it running against new artifacts, there's no way to detect whether a redeploy (e.g. a quantized export or dependency bump) silently regressed the metric that justified shipping the model
Eval harnesses cannot run outside of Jupyter notebooks
It removes the need for a model card entirely
questions.explain: The eval harness is what computed the originally reported score. Re-running it in CI before every redeploy is the only way a later silent regression gets caught before it reaches production.

questions.q: Why is a resolved (fully-expanded) config needed instead of just the override flags someone typed on the command line?
options: Override flags take up more disk space than a full config
The resolved config captures every hyperparameter that actually ran, including defaults the override flags didn't mention, so nothing is left to reconstruct from memory
Hydra cannot produce a resolved config, only override flags
Override flags are encrypted and cannot be logged
questions.explain: A handful of override flags omits every default value that was still in effect. The resolved, fully-expanded config is what the run actually used, with nothing implicit left out.

questions.q: Why does data version matter as a separate piece of lineage, alongside commit hash and config?
options: It doesn't; code and config alone fully determine a trained model
The same code and the same config can still produce a different model if run against a different version of the training data
Data version is only relevant for unsupervised learning, not supervised models
Data versioning replaces the need for a commit hash entirely
questions.explain: Code and config describe the recipe, but training data is the ingredients. The same recipe against different data still produces a different trained model, so data version is a distinct, necessary piece of lineage.

questions.q: What is the purpose of bundling commit hash, config snapshot, data version, and eval score into a single production manifest?
options: To reduce the file size of the exported model artifact
So the model's full provenance is retrievable with one lookup stored alongside the artifact, instead of scattered across Slack threads and people's memory
To replace the need for an eval harness
Manifests are required by ONNX and have no other purpose
questions.explain: The manifest's value is consolidation: lineage, eval results, and export details in one place next to the model, so reading the model's history is the same action as loading it.
